```{=html}
<header class="dg-head dg-head-section"><p class="dg-kicker">Chapter 2 <span class="dg-sep">•</span> <a href="index.html">Vector Spaces</a></p><h1 class="dg-title"><span class="dg-secnum">2.3</span> Bases, Components, and Transformation Laws</h1></header>
<p>Introducing a basis for a vector space allows us to express vectors, covectors, and tensors in terms of components. This leads to the explicit study of how vectors, covectors, and tensors transform under changes of basis, and how their components encode the abstract multilinear structures defined previously (row 5 of Figure <a class="dg-xref" href="../introduction/roadmaps.html#fig_vector_spaces_roadmap" data-kind="figure" data-label="fig_vector_spaces_roadmap">1.2</a>). Check appendices <a class="dg-xref" href="../examples/example-vector-space.html#subsection_appendix_example_vector_space_basis" data-kind="subsection" data-label="subsection_appendix_example_vector_space_basis">C.1.3</a> &amp; <a class="dg-xref" href="../examples/example-vector-space.html#subsection_appendix_example_vector_space_change_basis" data-kind="subsection" data-label="subsection_appendix_example_vector_space_change_basis">C.1.4</a> for concrete examples showing how to extract coordinate components, and how to work with different bases.</p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>Given a vector space <span class="math inline">\((V, \oplus, \odot)\)</span>, a subset <span class="math inline">\( B \subseteq V \)</span> is a (Hamel-)<sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-5" id="fnref-5" aria-label="Footnote 5">5</a></sup> <span class="dg-term dg-term-orange">basis</span> if  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \forall \mathcal{X} \in V, \, \exists ! \text{ finite }
            \{ \hat{x}_1, ..., \hat{x}_d \} \subset B :
            \exists ! \{ x^1, ..., x^d\} \in \mathbb{R} : \mathcal{X} = (x^1 \cdot \hat{x}_1) \oplus ...
            \oplus (x^d \cdot \hat{x}_d).
        \end{align*}</span>  If such a basis <span class="math inline">\(B\)</span> exists, we call <span class="math inline">\(d\)</span> the dimension of the vector space,and we say that <span class="math inline">\(\{ x^1, ..., x^d\}\)</span> are the <span class="dg-term dg-term-orange">components</span> of <span class="math inline">\(v\)</span> w.r.t <span class="math inline">\(B\)</span>.</p>
<p>Hence, we can decompose any vector <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X} \in V\)</span> as  <span class="math display">\[
            \mathcal{X} = \sum_{i=1}^d x^i \cdot \hat{x}_i
        \]</span>  where <span class="math inline">\(x^i \in \mathbb{R}\)</span> are the components of <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}\)</span> w.r.t <span class="math inline">\(B\)</span>.</p></li>
<li><p>Let <span class="math inline">\(\{\hat{x}_1, \dots, \hat{x}_d\}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\{\hat{y}_1, \dots, \hat{y}_d\}\)</span> be two bases of a vector space <span class="math inline">\((V, \oplus, \odot)\)</span>. Since both are bases, each vector of one basis can be uniquely expressed as a linear combination of the other. Therefore, there exists a matrix of real numbers <span class="math inline">\(J^j_{i}\)</span> such that:  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \hat{x}_i = \sum_{j=1}^d J^j_{i} \cdot \hat{y}_j , \quad \forall i = 1, \dots, d.
        \end{align*}</span>  We say that <span class="dg-term dg-term-orange">covariant</span> objects follow this transformation law, and the matrix <span class="math inline">\(J\)</span> defines the <span class="dg-term dg-term-orange">change of basis</span> between <span class="math inline">\(\{\hat{x}_i\}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\{\hat{y}_i\}\)</span>.</p>
<p>The matrix <span class="math inline">\(J^j_{i} \)</span> is invertible– meaning that there exists a matrix <span class="math inline">\((J^{-1})^j_{i}\)</span> such that<sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-6" id="fnref-6" aria-label="Footnote 6">6</a></sup> <span class="math inline">\(J^i_{j} \cdot (J^{-1})^j_{i} = \delta^j_i\)</span> – which is a direct consequence of the fact that both sets <span class="math inline">\(\{\hat{x}_i\}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\{\hat{y}_i\}\)</span> are linearly independent and span the same vector space <span class="math inline">\(V\)</span>. Therefore, the inverse transformation law reads:  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \hat{y}_i = \sum_{j=1}^d (J^{-1})^j_{i} \cdot \hat{x}_j, \quad \forall i = 1, \dots, d.
        \end{align*}</span></p></li>
<li><p>Let <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X} \in V\)</span> be a vector with components <span class="math inline">\(\{x^i\}\)</span> relative to the basis <span class="math inline">\(\{\hat{x}_i\}\)</span> and components <span class="math inline">\(\{y^i\}\)</span> relative to the basis <span class="math inline">\(\{\hat{y}_i\}\)</span>. The decomposition of <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}\)</span> w.r.t. both bases reads:  <span class="math display">\[
            \mathcal{X} = \sum_{i=1}^d x^i \cdot \hat{x}_i = \sum_{i=1}^d y^i \cdot \hat{y}_i.
        \]</span></p>
<p>Plugging the change of basis relation this expression gives:  <span class="math display">\[
            \mathcal{X} = \sum_{i=1}^d x^i \cdot \sum_{j=1}^d J^j_{i} \cdot \hat{y}_j
            = \sum_{i=1}^d y^i \cdot \hat{y}_i.
        \]</span>  Since the basis vectors are linearly independent, we can equate the components on both sides to obtain the transformation law for the vector components:  <span class="math display">\[
            y^i = \sum_{j=1}^d J^i_{j} \cdot x^j
            \longrightarrow
            x^i = \sum_{j=1}^d (J^{-1})^i_{j} \cdot y^j.
        \]</span>  We say that <span class="dg-term dg-term-orange">contravariant</span> objects follow this transformation law.</p></li>
<li><p>Given a basis <span class="math inline">\(B\coloneq \{ \hat{x}_1, ..., \hat{x}_d \}\)</span> of a vector space <span class="math inline">\((V, \oplus, \odot)\)</span>, we can define (it’s a convenient choice) the <span class="dg-term dg-term-red">induced dual cobasis</span> <span class="math inline">\(B^* \coloneq \{\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^1, ..., \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^d\}\)</span> of its dual vector space <span class="math inline">\((V^*, \oplus^*, \odot^*)\)</span> as  :  <span class="math display">\[
            \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i (\hat{x}_j) = \delta^i_j =
            \begin{cases}
                1 &amp; \text{if } i = j, \\
                0 &amp; \text{otherwise}.
            \end{cases}
        \]</span></p>
<p>Hence, we can decompose any covector <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X} \in V^*\)</span> as  <span class="math display">\[
            \mathsf{X} = \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}_i \cdot \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i
        \]</span>  where <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}\)</span> are the components of <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}\)</span> w.r.t <span class="math inline">\(B^*\)</span>.</p></li>
<li><p>Let <span class="math inline">\(B_1^* \coloneq \{\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^1, \dots, \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^d\}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(B_2^* \coloneq \{\hat{\mathfrak{y}}^1, \dots, \hat{\mathfrak{y}}^d\}\)</span> be the dual bases associated to the bases <span class="math inline">\(B_1 \coloneq \{\hat{x}_1, \dots, \hat{x}_d\}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(B_2 \coloneq \{\hat{y}_1, \dots, \hat{y}_d\}\)</span>, respectively. Since both are dual bases, each covector of one basis can be uniquely expressed as a linear combination of the other. Therefore, there exists a matrix of real numbers <span class="math inline">\(J^i_{j}\)</span> (the same as for the vectors<sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-7" id="fnref-7" aria-label="Footnote 7">7</a></sup>) such that:  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i = \sum_{j=1}^d (J^{-1})^i_{j} \cdot \hat{\mathfrak{y}}^j
            \longrightarrow
            \hat{\mathfrak{y}}^i = \sum_{j=1}^d J^i_{j} \cdot \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^j,
            \quad \forall i = 1, \dots, d.
        \end{align*}</span>  As we previously defined it, we can observe that this transformation corresponds to that of a contravariant object.</p></li>
<li><p>Let <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X} \in V^*\)</span> be a covector with components <span class="math inline">\(\{\mathtt{x}^i\}\)</span> relative to the basis <span class="math inline">\(\{\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i\}\)</span>, and components <span class="math inline">\(\{\mathtt{y}^i\}\)</span> relative to the basis <span class="math inline">\(\{\hat{\mathfrak{y}}^i\}\)</span>. The decomposition of <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}\)</span> w.r.t. both bases reads:  <span class="math display">\[
            \mathsf{X} = \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}_i \cdot \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i
            = \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{y}_i \cdot \hat{\mathfrak{y}}^i.
        \]</span>  Plugging the change of basis relation into this expression gives:  <span class="math display">\[
            \mathsf{X} = \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}_i \cdot \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i
            = \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{y}_i \cdot \sum_{j=1}^d J^i_{j} \cdot \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^j.
        \]</span>  Since the basis vectors are linearly independent, we can equate the components on both sides to obtain the transformation law for the covector components:  <span class="math display">\[
            \mathtt{x}_j = \sum_{i=1}^d J^i_{j} \cdot \mathtt{y}_i
            \longrightarrow
            \mathtt{y}_j = \sum_{i=1}^d (J^{-1})^i_{j} \cdot \mathtt{x}_i.
        \]</span>  Hence, we can observe that covector components transform as covariant objects.</p></li>
<li><p>Let <span class="math inline">\(\left\{ \hat{x}_1, \dots, \hat{x}_d \right\}\)</span> be a basis of the vector space <span class="math inline">\((V, \oplus, \odot)\)</span>, and <span class="math inline">\(\left\{ \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^1, \dots, \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^d \right\}\)</span> its associated dual basis in <span class="math inline">\((V^*, \oplus^*, \odot^*)\)</span>. Then the <span class="math inline">\(d^{\,r+s}\)</span> tensors  <span class="math display">\[
            \left\{
            \hat{x}_{i_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \hat{x}_{i_r} \otimes
            \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{j_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{j_s}
            \;\Big|\;
            i_1,\dots,i_r, j_1,\dots,j_s \in \{1,\dots,d\}
            \right\}
        \]</span>  constitute a <span class="dg-term dg-term-brown">basis of <span class="math inline">\(T^{(r,s)}\)</span></span>. By the slot-by-slot action of simple tensors defined above, and <span class="math inline">\(\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{k}(\hat{x}_{i}) = \delta^{k}_{i}\)</span>, each of them evaluates on basis elements as  <span class="math display">\begin{equation*}
            \left( \hat{x}_{i_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \hat{x}_{i_r} \otimes
            \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{j_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{j_s} \right)
            \left( \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{k_1}, \dots, \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{k_r};
            \hat{x}_{l_1}, \dots, \hat{x}_{l_s} \right)
            = \delta^{k_1}_{i_1} \cdots \delta^{k_r}_{i_r} \cdot \delta^{j_1}_{l_1} \cdots \delta^{j_s}_{l_s}.
            \tag{$\star$}
        \end{equation*}</span>  <em>Proof</em>:</p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-2">
<li><p>Spanning: Given <span class="math inline">\(T \in T^{(r,s)}\)</span>, define its <span class="dg-term dg-term-brown">components</span> by evaluation on the basis,  <span class="math display">\[
                    T^{i_1 \dots i_r}_{j_1 \dots j_s}
                    \coloneqq T \left(
                    \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{i_1}, \dots, \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{i_r};
                    \hat{x}_{j_1}, \dots, \hat{x}_{j_s}
                    \right) \in \mathbb{R},
                \]</span>  and consider  <span class="math display">\[
                    S \coloneqq \sum_{\substack{i_1,\dots,i_r \\ j_1,\dots,j_s}}
                    T^{i_1\dots i_r}_{j_1\dots j_s}
                    \cdot \hat{x}_{i_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \hat{x}_{i_r}
                    \otimes \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{j_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{j_s}.
                \]</span>  By <span class="math inline">\((\star)\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(S\left( \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{k_1}, \dots, \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{k_r}; \hat{x}_{l_1}, \dots, \hat{x}_{l_s} \right) = T^{k_1\dots k_r}_{l_1\dots l_s} = T\left( \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{k_1}, \dots, \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{k_r}; \hat{x}_{l_1}, \dots, \hat{x}_{l_s} \right)\)</span> for every choice of indices. Two multilinear maps that agree on all tuples of basis elements agree everywhere (expand each argument in its basis and use multilinearity slot by slot), hence <span class="math inline">\(T = S\)</span>.</p></li>
<li><p>Linear independence: Suppose a linear combination of these tensors vanishes:  <span class="math display">\[
                    \sum_{\substack{i_1,\dots,i_r \\ j_1,\dots,j_s}}
                    \alpha^{i_1\dots i_r}_{j_1\dots j_s}
                    \cdot \hat{x}_{i_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \hat{x}_{i_r}
                    \otimes \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{j_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{j_s} = 0.
                \]</span>  Evaluating both sides on <span class="math inline">\(\left( \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{k_1}, \dots, \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{k_r}; \hat{x}_{l_1}, \dots, \hat{x}_{l_s} \right)\)</span> and using <span class="math inline">\((\star)\)</span>, every term vanishes except the one with <span class="math inline">\(i_1 = k_1, \dots, j_s = l_s\)</span>, which yields <span class="math inline">\(\alpha^{k_1\dots k_r}_{l_1\dots l_s} = 0\)</span> for all index combinations.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>Hence every <span class="math inline">\(T \in T^{(r,s)}\)</span> decomposes uniquely as  <span class="math display">\[
            T = \sum_{\substack{i_1,\dots,i_r \\ j_1,\dots,j_s}}
            T^{i_1\dots i_r}_{j_1\dots j_s}
            \cdot \hat{x}_{i_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \hat{x}_{i_r}
            \otimes \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{j_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \hat{\mathfrak{x}}^{j_s},
            \qquad \dim T^{(r,s)} = d^{\,r+s}.
        \]</span></p></li>
<li><p>A tensor <span class="math inline">\(T\)</span> acts on any collection of <span class="math inline">\(r\)</span> covectors <span class="math inline">\(\{\mathsf{X}^{(i)}\}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(s\)</span> vectors <span class="math inline">\(\{\mathcal{X}^{(j)}\}\)</span> as:  <span class="math display">\[
            \begin{aligned}
                T \left( \mathsf{X}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathsf{X}^{(r)},
                \mathcal{X}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathcal{X}^{(s)} \right) =
                \sum_{\substack{i_1,\dots,i_r \\ j_1,\dots,j_s}}
                T^{i_1 \dots i_r}_{j_1 \dots j_s} \cdot
                \mathtt{x}_{i_1} \dots \mathtt{x}_{i_r}
                \cdot x^{j_1} \dots x^{j_s}.
            \end{aligned}
        \]</span></p></li>
<li><p>The components of a tensor <span class="math inline">\(T \in T^{(r,s)}\)</span> transform according to:  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            {T}^{i_1 \dots i_r}_{j_1 \dots j_s}
            &amp;=
            \sum_{\substack{k_1,\dots,k_r \\ l_1,\dots,l_s}}
            \left[
            (J^{-1})^{i_1}_{k_1} \dots (J^{-1})^{i_r}_{k_r}
            \cdot
            J^{l_1}_{j_1} \dots J^{l_s}_{j_s}
            \cdot
            \widetilde{{T}}^{k_1 \dots k_r}_{l_1 \dots l_s}
            \right],\\
            \widetilde{T}^{i_1 \dots i_r}_{j_1 \dots j_s}
            &amp;=
            \sum_{\substack{k_1,\dots,k_r \\ l_1,\dots,l_s}}
            \left[
            J^{i_1}_{k_1} \dots J^{i_r}_{k_r}
            \cdot
            (J^{-1})^{l_1}_{j_1} \dots (J^{-1})^{l_s}_{j_s}
            \cdot
            {T}^{k_1 \dots k_r}_{l_1 \dots l_s}
            \right],
        \end{align*}</span>  where <span class="math inline">\({T}\)</span> are the components in the <span class="math inline">\(\{\hat{\mathfrak{x}}^i, \hat{x}_j\}\)</span> basis and <span class="math inline">\(\widetilde{{T}}\)</span> are the components in the <span class="math inline">\(\{\hat{\mathfrak{y}}^i, \hat{y}_j\}\)</span> basis.</p>
<p>This generalizes the transformation rules previously seen for vectors (contravariant) and covectors (covariant).</p></li>
</ul>
<div class="dg-footnotes"><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-5"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-5" aria-label="Back to the text">5</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p>See Appendix <a class="dg-xref" href="../proofs-and-additional-material/hamel-schauder.html" data-kind="section" data-label="appendix_Hamel_Schauder">B.2</a> for a discussion on finite versus infinite bases (Hamel vs. Schauder).</p></div></div><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-6"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-6" aria-label="Back to the text">6</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p>Where <span class="math inline">\(\delta^i_j\)</span> is the Kronecker delta, which is <span class="math inline">\(1\)</span> if <span class="math inline">\(i=j\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(0\)</span> otherwise.</p></div></div><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-7"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-7" aria-label="Back to the text">7</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p>A formal proof that the change-of-basis matrix for the dual bases is indeed the same matrix <span class="math inline">\(J\)</span> used for the vectors is provided in Appendix <a class="dg-xref" href="../proofs-and-additional-material/proof-dual-basis-transformation.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_proof_dual_basis_transformation">B.3</a>.</p></div></div></div>
```
